narrative:
The model estimates you have a 24% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of passing.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. First, the fact that you want to pursue higher education actually works against you here. Every student who passed expressed the same ambition, so your “no” answer stands out sharply and pulls the prediction toward failure. Second, you have already failed three classes in the past. This is far above the average of zero failures among students who passed, and it strongly pushes the model to expect you will struggle again. Third, although you are receiving extra educational support at school, this factor surprisingly pulls the prediction slightly toward passing. In the data, almost no one who passed needed this support, so the model sees it as a mild positive signal that is not enough to outweigh the other two influences.

To improve, focus on two things. Talk with your teachers about why past classes did not work out and create a realistic plan to avoid repeating those patterns. At the same time, reconnect with your goal of higher education; use that motivation to set weekly study targets above your current level of less than two hours. Small, consistent changes in these areas can shift your trajectory before the final exams.
